title: Women among the five
hook: some gurdwaras include women among the Panj Pyare, some do not, and Sikhs discuss it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth question: views differ on who wrote parts of it, and Jaap Sahib and Chaupai are shared. Your line was shared devotion.

An amrit ceremony, in a closed room. Five initiated Sikhs in saffron stand around an iron bowl of water, stirring it with a double-edged khanda while they recite. They are the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, standing in for the first five who answered the Guru's call. In one city, one of the five today is a woman. In another city, at another gurdwara, the five are always men. Both are Sikh ceremonies. Today is the conversation between them.
screen: `FIVE IN SAFFRON, ONE IRON BOWL.` → `IN ONE CITY, A WOMAN AMONG THEM.` → `IN ANOTHER, ALWAYS MEN.`

segments.voice: Begin with the story this path told on day eighty-four. Tradition says that at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked the gathered Sikhs who would give their head, and five men stepped forward one by one. They became the first Panj Pyare and received the first amrit. Tradition also says that Mata Sahib Kaur came and added sugar sweets to the water, so the amrit would carry sweetness along with the steel. So the first five were men, and a woman's hand is in the bowl. Here the views part. Some Sikhs hold that the five should follow the first five, and that the ceremony keeps its shape best by keeping its history. Others point to the Sikh code of conduct, whose readers say its section on the amrit ceremony allows Sikh women to be among the five. And they point to a line from the Asa di Var that this path met on the phulkari day. On Ang 473, Guru Nanak asks, here in paraphrase, why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? Here it's read as a question about who may stand at the bowl. In practice, some gurdwaras now include women among the Panj Pyare, and some do not. Both sides take the ceremony seriously, which is exactly why they care. The disagreement isn't about whether amrit matters. It's about how faithfully to keep a picture of the first day, and what faithfulness asks. Sikhs keep discussing it in gurdwara committees, in homes and online, and meanwhile the ceremony is held both ways.
screen: `FIVE MEN STEPPED FORWARD.` · `A WOMAN'S HAND IN THE BOWL.` · `THE CODE AND ANG 473.` · `TWO PRACTICES, ONE CEREMONY.` · then, large: `WHAT DOES FAITHFULNESS ASK?`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation in your own life that isn't finished, in your family, your work or your faith community, and don't try to win it or end it; just notice where it lives and whether it's still being held kindly. Then choose one small thing that would keep it open next time: a question, a pause, a cup of tea.
Women among the five. Some gurdwaras include women among the Panj Pyare who serve amrit, some do not, and Sikhs are still talking it through. Today's word.
Your line: the conversation continues. The bowl is the same, and the talk goes on. See you tomorrow.

No. The first amrit had no woman's part at all, so no gurdwara includes women.
Yes. Every gurdwara must now include a woman, by direct order of the code.
